I coach people who go to business events, and I always hear the same problem. They know how to start a conversation, but after the first answer, there is an awkward silence. The most common mistake is to ask one closed question after another, like an interview. Do you like the event? Yes. Is it your first time? Yes. Are you staying long? No. That is not a conversation. So here is my advice. First, comment on the answer before you ask again. Second, use follow-up questions. If someone says they just arrived from Colombia, ask how the flight was, or what they think of the city. A follow-up question shows that you are really listening. Third, use a question tag to invite the other person in. Great talk, wasn't it? Let your voice go down at the end, and people will agree and keep talking. And when it is time to leave, do not just disappear. Excuse yourself with a reason, and suggest a next step, like exchanging business cards. People will remember you as someone who was easy to talk to.

A few years ago, my flight from Rotterdam was delayed for five hours. I was tired and a little angry, and I sat down at the coffee shop near the gate. The man next to me looked at the screen and sighed. So I said, long delay, isn't it? He laughed and said, the third one this month. We started talking about the weather, then about travel, and then I asked him what he did. He was a buyer for a roaster in Germany. I said, you buy Brazilian coffee, don't you? He did, and he was looking for a new supplier. It was a small world, because he knew two of my clients in Santos. We exchanged business cards before the flight. Two months later, we signed a contract for a container of coffee. Today I always tell young traders: never waste a coffee break, and never waste a delay.
